entry:
Mechanical device that changes the direction or magnitude of a force. The term usually refers to the six classical simple machines defined by Renaissance scientists: the [[Lever|lever]], [[Wheel and axle]], [[Pulley|pulley]], [[Inclined plane|inclined plane]], [[Wedge|wedge]], and [[Screw|screw]]. A simple machine uses a single applied force to do work against a single load force. Ignoring friction losses, the work done on the load equals the work done by the applied force, so a machine can increase output force only at the cost of a proportional decrease in the distance the load moves. The ratio of output force to applied force is the mechanical advantage. Some machines, such as a stationary pulley, only change the direction of the force.

Simple machines can be regarded as elementary building blocks of compound machines; a bicycle, for example, uses wheels, levers, and pulleys. The mechanical advantage of a compound machine is the product of the advantages of its component simple machines.

The idea originated with the Greek philosopher [[Archimedes]] around the 3rd century BC, who studied the lever, pulley, and screw and discovered the principle of mechanical advantage in the lever. Heron of Alexandria (c. 10–75 AD) listed five mechanisms: lever, windlass, pulley, wedge, and screw. Greek understanding was limited to statics, without the tradeoff between force and distance or the concept of work. In 1586 the Flemish engineer Simon Stevin derived the mechanical advantage of the inclined plane. The Italian scientist [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] worked out the complete dynamic theory in 1600 in *Le Mecaniche*, showing that simple machines do not create energy, only transform it.

Modern mechanics has moved beyond treating the six machines as the ultimate building blocks. By the late 1800s Franz Reuleaux had identified hundreds of machine elements, and modern machine theory analyzes machines as kinematic chains of elementary linkages called kinematic pairs.

Island country and city-state in Southeast Asia (pop., 2025: 6.11 million), off the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. Its territory comprises a main island, over 60 satellite islands and islets, and one outlying islet, about one degree of latitude (137 km) north of the equator. It is bordered by the Strait of Malacca to the west, the Singapore Strait to the south, the South China Sea to the east, and the Straits of Johor to the north, beyond which lies the Malaysian state of Johor.

In early history the island was a maritime emporium known as Temasek. Its contemporary era began in 1819, when Stamford Raffles established it as a trading post of the British Empire; it came under direct British control in 1867 as part of the Straits Settlements. Japan occupied it in 1942, and it returned to Britain as a Crown colony in 1945. Singapore gained self-governance in 1959 and in 1963 joined the new federation of Malaysia. Ideological differences led to its expulsion two years later, and it became independent on August 9, 1965.

Singapore is a parliamentary republic with a legal system based on common law. The People's Action Party has held power continuously since 1959; supporters credit its policies of meritocracy and rule of law, including the leadership of Lee Kuan Yew, while critics note limited political pluralism and laws restricting free speech and assembly. It has four official languages: English, Malay, Mandarin, and Tamil.

Despite lacking natural resources, the country became one of the Four Asian Tigers and a major financial, aviation, and shipping hub. It has the highest PPP-adjusted GDP per capita in the world and the second highest population density of any country. It is a founding member of ASEAN.

Art of creating music with the human voice. Often called the oldest form of musical expression, it is performed with or without instrumental accompaniment, by soloists or in ensembles such as a choir, and ranges from a single accompanying instrument to a symphony orchestra or big band. It may be formal or informal, arranged or improvised, and serves religious devotion, ritual, pleasure, comfort, education, or profession. Many styles exist throughout the world.

Physically, singing depends on the lungs, which supply air; the larynx, which acts as a vibrator; the chest, head cavities, and skeleton, which amplify the sound; and the tongue, palate, teeth, and lips, which shape consonants and vowels. Pitch is altered with the vocal cords. Each person's voice is unique, shaped by the vocal cords and by the size and shape of the whole body. Singers can learn to project sound so that it resonates better in the vocal tract, and different functions of the larynx produce different vocal registers, such as chest, head, and falsetto. Vocal folds vibrate at frequencies from 60 to 2000 Hz.

In European classical music and [[Opera|opera]], voices are treated like instruments and classified by range, weight, tessitura, and timbre into types such as soprano, mezzo-soprano, contralto, tenor, baritone, and bass. Professional singers usually specialize in one genre, such as classical or rock, and typically train throughout their careers with vocal coaches or teachers.

Singing is distinguished from [[Rapping|rapping]], which does not require pitch accuracy and uses rhythmic speech rather than sung pitches, although some rap artists alternate between the two. Group singing predominates in most cultures, in religious rituals, dances, and community bonding.

Structural frame that supports the body of most animals. The main types are the exoskeleton, a rigid outer shell; the endoskeleton, a rigid internal frame to which organs and soft tissues attach; and the hydroskeleton, a flexible structure supported by the hydrostatic pressure of body fluids. The word comes from Ancient Greek *skeletós*, "dried up." Skeletons may also be classed as pliant or rigid, depending on whether they deform under stress and regain their shape.

Exoskeletons cover the body, protect against predators, and provide surfaces for muscle attachment. [[Arthropod|Arthropods]] must periodically molt as they grow, and the shells of mollusks are another form. Because an external skeleton is heavy relative to body mass, land animals with one are mostly small, while larger forms live in water. Rigid skeletons are built from materials such as [[Chitin|chitin]] in arthropods, calcium carbonate in stony corals and mollusks, and silicate in diatoms and radiolarians.

Endoskeletons are composed of mineralized tissues and occur in chordates, echinoderms, and sponges. They range from purely supportive structures, as in sponges, to attachment sites that transmit muscular forces. [[Vertebrate|Vertebrate]] skeletons are endoskeletons centered on an axial vertebral column and made mainly of [[Bone|bone]] and [[Cartilage|cartilage]]. The [[Human skeleton|human skeleton]] has 206 bones in adults, which fuse from about 270 at birth, and also serves as a reservoir for minerals and a site of blood cell production.

Hydrostatic skeletons are muscle- and connective-tissue-walled cavities of fluid found in soft-bodied animals such as jellyfish, flatworms, nematodes, and earthworms; alternating muscle contractions let the animal move. Invertebrate skeletons vary widely, including plated internal shells, ossicles, and the spicules of [[Sponge|sponges]]. The cytoskeleton serves a similar function at the cellular level.

Soft, flexible outer tissue covering the body of a [[Vertebrate|vertebrate]] animal, with three main functions: protection, regulation, and sensation. In [[Mammal|mammals]] it is an organ of the [[Integumentary system|integumentary system]] made of multiple layers of ectodermal tissue, guarding the underlying muscles, bones, ligaments, and internal organs. Other animal coverings, such as the arthropod exoskeleton, differ in origin, structure, and chemistry.

The skin is the first line of defense against the environment, protecting against pathogens and excessive water loss. It also provides insulation, regulates temperature, and produces vitamin D. Severely damaged skin may heal by forming scar tissue, and healing is promoted by estrogen. Thickness varies: in humans the skin around the eyelids is thinnest at 0.5 mm, and that on the palms and soles is thickest at 4 mm.

Mammalian skin has two primary layers. The epidermis provides waterproofing and a barrier to infection. It is a stratified squamous epithelium in which keratinocytes, which make up 95% of the epidermis, proliferate in the basal layer by mitosis, move upward, and are eventually shed from the surface. It contains no blood vessels and is nourished by diffusion from capillaries in the dermis. The dermis lies beneath it, consists of connective tissue, cushions the body from stress and strain, and gives the skin tensile strength and elasticity through collagen and elastic fibers. A thin basement membrane separates the two layers.

Skin differs among groups. All mammals have some hair, and [[Fur|fur]] augments insulation. Reptiles and most fish have scales, and birds have feathers, all made of beta-keratins. Amphibian skin is a weak barrier and permits the passage of chemicals. Thick animal skin can be processed into [[Leather|leather]]. The oldest known skin, possibly from an ancient reptile, was fossilized about 289 million years ago.

Ownership of a person as property, especially in regard to their labor. Slavery typically involves compulsory work, with the location of work and residence dictated by the party holding the person in bondage. Enslavement occurred through law-breaking, debt, military defeat, or exploitation for cheaper labor, and some forms were instituted along lines of race or sex. Slaves were held for life or for a fixed period. Although usually involuntary, there were cases of people entering slavery voluntarily to pay a debt. In chattel slavery, the slave is legally the personal property of the owner and can be bought and sold. Historians disagree on whether terms such as "enslaved person" should replace "slave"; proponents say the older term reduces victims to a nonhuman noun, while others prefer it as familiar and as reflecting slavery's inhumanity.

Slavery existed in most societies and was a common feature of civilization. It was a keystone of society in ancient Greece and the [[Roman Empire]], and was practiced in the medieval Muslim world, sub-Saharan Africa, the Caribbean, and the antebellum United States. The transatlantic trade carried about 12 million Africans to the Americas between 1500 and 1866.

From the 18th century, [[Abolitionism|abolitionist]] movements in Europe and the Americas condemned slavery as a violation of human rights. After the [[French Revolution]] France abolished slavery in 1794, Napoleon reintroduced it in 1802, and permanent abolition came in 1848. Slavery was abolished in much of the [[British Empire]] in 1833, throughout the United States in 1865, in [[Cuba]] in 1886, and in [[Brazil]], the last country in the Americas to do so, in 1888.

Slavery is now outlawed in every country except as punishment for a crime, but persists in some form everywhere. In 2019 approximately 40 million people, 26% of them children, were enslaved, most often in forced labor, debt bondage, forced marriage, or [[Human trafficking|human trafficking]].

Naturally recurring state of reduced mental and physical activity in which [[Consciousness|consciousness]] is altered and certain sensory activity is inhibited. Muscle activity and interaction with the surroundings decrease markedly, yet sleep involves active brain patterns and is more reactive than a coma. Sleeping persons perceive fewer stimuli but can generally still respond to loud noises.

Sleep occurs in repeating cycles that alternate between non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. NREM, divided by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine into stages N1, N2, and N3, comes first; N3 is also called slow-wave or deep sleep, during which body temperature and heart rate fall and growth hormone is secreted in bursts. REM sleep is the main occasion for [[Dream|dreams]] and is marked by fast brain waves, eye movements, and loss of muscle tone. A cycle averages 90 minutes and occurs 4–6 times in a good night's sleep. The internal [[Circadian rhythm|circadian]] clock promotes sleep at night.

The brain uses significantly less energy during sleep; in quiet waking it accounts for 20% of the body's energy use. Most body systems are in an anabolic state, restoring the immune, nervous, skeletal, and muscular systems and supporting mood, memory, and cognitive function. The purposes of sleep remain under active research. It is highly conserved across animal evolution, and researchers have found that cleansing the brain of waste, including amyloid, may be a core purpose. Sleep is studied by electroencephalography (EEG), eye-movement and muscle recordings, and polysomnography in sleep laboratories.

Sleep disorders include [[Insomnia|insomnia]], hypersomnia, [[Narcolepsy|narcolepsy]], [[Sleep apnea|sleep apnea]], sleepwalking, and REM sleep behavior disorder. Artificial light, including the blue light of digital screens, has altered human sleep patterns by disrupting release of the hormone melatonin.

Infectious disease caused by the variola virus, genus *Orthopoxvirus*, and the only human disease to have been eradicated. The last naturally occurring case was diagnosed in October 1977, and the [[World Health Organization]] certified global eradication in 1980.

Initial symptoms were fever and vomiting, followed by mouth ulcers and a skin rash. Over days the rash turned into fluid-filled blisters with a central dent, which scabbed over and fell off, leaving scars. Transmission was primarily through prolonged face-to-face contact with an infected person, rarely through contaminated objects. Variola major, the severe and more common form, carried a death risk of about 30%, higher among babies; variola minor was milder, with historical death rates of 1% or less. Survivors often had extensive scarring, and some were left blind.

The earliest evidence dates to about 1500 BC in Egyptian mummies. The disease was among those introduced to the New World by the [[Columbian exchange]], killing large numbers of Native Americans. In 18th-century Europe an estimated 400,000 people died of it each year, and one-third of all blindness was due to smallpox. It is estimated to have killed up to 300 million people in the 20th century and around 500 million in its last 100 years. As recently as 1967, 15 million cases occurred a year.

Inoculation appears to have begun in China around the 1500s, and Europe adopted it from Asia in the first half of the 18th century. In 1796 [[Edward Jenner]] introduced the modern [[Smallpox vaccine|smallpox vaccine]]. In 1967 the WHO intensified its eradication campaign, using ring vaccination of contacts of cases. Samples of the virus are now confined to two secure laboratories. The only other disease eradicated is rinderpest, in 2011. The term "smallpox" was first used in England in the 16th century to distinguish it from [[Syphilis|syphilis]], then called the "great pox."

Combustion of a substance, usually plant material, and inhalation of the resulting fumes. It is practiced mainly as a route of administration for psychoactive chemicals, which vaporize and are rapidly absorbed through the lungs into the bloodstream, reaching the central nervous system. Tobacco smoking, the most popular form, is practiced by over one billion people, most of them in developing countries. In tobacco the active substance is [[Nicotine|nicotine]], an alkaloid carried in aerosol particles. Other drugs smoked include [[Cannabis|cannabis]], [[Opium|opium]], morphine, cocaine, and methamphetamine.

Tobacco is smoked mostly as [[Cigarette|cigarettes]], which are industrially manufactured or hand-rolled, but also in pipes, cigars, bidis, hookahs, and bongs. Most cigarette smokers inhale; most pipe and cigar smokers do not.

Smoking dates to as early as 5000 BC and appears in many cultures, where it was associated with religious ceremonies, offerings to deities, cleansing rituals, and shamanic divination. After European contact with the Americas, tobacco smoking spread quickly worldwide. In India and [[Sub-Saharan Africa]] it merged with existing smoking practices, mostly of cannabis. Attitudes have varied between places and eras, from holy to sinful and from panacea to health hazard; by the late 20th century smoking was viewed negatively, especially in Western countries.

Smoking is among the leading causes of [[Lung cancer|lung cancer]], heart attack, [[Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease]], erectile dysfunction, and birth defects. Related diseases are shown to kill approximately half of long-term smokers. It is estimated to kill more than seven million people worldwide each year, including 1.6 million non-smokers exposed to passive smoke. In the United States about 480,000 die annually. Many countries respond by taxing tobacco heavily, publishing anti-smoking advertising, limiting or banning tobacco advertising, and helping smokers quit.

Solid atmospheric [[Precipitation|precipitation]] consisting of individual ice crystals that grow while suspended in the air, usually within clouds, then fall and accumulate on the ground. Snow is frozen crystalline water throughout its life cycle: crystals form in the atmosphere, grow to millimeter size, precipitate, accumulate, then metamorphose in place and finally melt, slide, or sublimate away.

Snowflakes nucleate around particles in the atmosphere by attracting supercooled water droplets, which freeze into hexagonal crystals. Basic shapes include platelets, needles, columns, and rime. Snow clouds usually occur within larger weather systems, chiefly the [[Low-pressure area|low-pressure area]], with its warm and cold fronts. Cold fronts can produce intense snowsqualls with whiteout conditions, usually lasting under 30 minutes at any point; warm fronts produce snow where warm, moist air overrides below-freezing air. Two other productive sources are lake-effect snow, produced when cold air crosses warmer water and deposits snow on downwind shores, and orographic snowfall, created when moist air is forced up mountains. Snowbelts include areas east of the [[Great Lakes]], the west coast of northern Japan, and the Kamchatka Peninsula.

Accumulated snow, or snowpack, may blow into drifts and changes over time by sintering, sublimation, and freeze-thaw. Where the climate is cold enough for year-to-year accumulation, a [[Glacier|glacier]] may form; otherwise snow melts seasonally, causing runoff into streams and rivers and recharging groundwater. Snow has high [[Albedo|albedo]], reflecting up to 90% of sunlight, and low thermal conductivity. It covers an average of 44 million sq km of the [[Northern Hemisphere]] each winter.

Major snow-prone areas are the polar regions, the northern half of the Northern Hemisphere, and mountains worldwide; in the Southern Hemisphere snow is largely confined to mountains and Antarctica. Snow affects transportation, agriculture, sports such as [[Skiing|skiing]], and warfare, and it insulates plants and animals through winter.
